name: Olivine
chronometers: Fe–Mg, Ni, Ca diffusion chronometry (magma timescales)

matrix.title: Tabular ↔ elongate × form complexity
matrix.subtitle: Rows run from crystals flattened on (010) to crystals elongated along [001]. Columns add the domes, dipyramid and minor prisms of polyhedral olivine phenocrysts.
matrix.note: All indices are in the Pbnm cell, which equals Dana's morphological axes. 8 interfacial angles match Dana (1892) to within 0.1°. Many diffusion papers use Pnma, where (hkl)<sub>Pbnm</sub> = (klh)<sub>Pnma</sub>. Which forms dominate follows the standard drawings, and aspect ratios are illustrative. Hopper, skeletal and dendritic olivine is not convex and is not modelled.

about:
Olivine's external shape records how fast it grew. Slowly cooled phenocrysts are polyhedral, combining {010}, {110}, {021}, {101} and {111}, while faster undercooling gives hopper, skeletal, chain and dendritic crystals (Donaldson 1976; Faure et al. 2003). Many polyhedral phenocrysts started as dendrites (Welsch et al. 2013, 2014).

3D shape matters directly for diffusion chronometry. Fe–Mg diffusion is fastest along [001], and a random 2D section through a 3D crystal can mislead the timescale estimate (Shea et al. 2015). The polyhedra here are the 3D shapes such sections cut through.

habits.name: Polyhedral phenocryst
habits.text: Equant to slightly elongate along [001], mildly flattened on (010); dominated by {010}, {110}, {021} (row Q).

habits.name: Tabular on (010)
habits.text: Dana: crystals often flattened parallel to b (rows T1–T2).

habits.name: Prismatic along [001]
habits.text: Gem peridot and forsterite: striated prisms with wedge-shaped {021}+{101} terminations (rows E1–E2).

habits.name: Not modelled
habits.text: Hopper, skeletal and dendritic crystals from rapid undercooling are not convex.

references.citation: Donaldson, C.H. (1976). An experimental investigation of olivine morphology. Contributions to Mineralogy and Petrology 57, 187–213.
references.note: The classic study of olivine morphology versus cooling rate: polyhedral → hopper → chain → dendrite.

references.citation: Faure, F., Trolliard, G., Nicollet, C., Montel, J.-M. (2003). A developmental model of olivine morphology as a function of the cooling rate and the degree of undercooling. Contributions to Mineralogy and Petrology 145, 251–263.
references.note: Morphology as a function of undercooling.

references.citation: Welsch, B., Faure, F., Famin, V., Baronnet, A., Bachèlery, P. (2013). Dendritic crystallization: a single process for all the textures of olivine in basalts? Journal of Petrology 54, 539–574.
references.note: Polyhedral phenocrysts can grow from dendrites.

references.citation: Welsch, B., Hammer, J., Hellebrand, E. (2014). Phosphorus zoning reveals dendritic architecture of olivine. Geology 42, 867–870.
references.note: Internal growth architecture versus external polyhedral habit.

references.citation: Shea, T., Costa, F., Krimer, D., Hammer, J.E. (2015). Accuracy of timescales retrieved from diffusion modeling in olivine: A 3D perspective. American Mineralogist 100, 2026–2042.
references.note: 3D crystal shape, sectioning and anisotropy effects on diffusion timescales. A direct motivation for 3D habit models.

references.citation: Costa, F., Dungan, M. (2005). Short time scales of magmatic assimilation from diffusion modeling of multiple elements in olivine. Geology 33, 837–840.

Dohmen, R., Chakraborty, S. (2007). Fe–Mg diffusion in olivine II: point defect chemistry, change of diffusion mechanisms and a model for calculation of diffusion coefficients in natural olivine. Physics and Chemistry of Minerals 34, 409–430.

Kirfel, A., Lippmann, T., Blaha, P., Schwarz, K., Cox, D.F., Rosso, K.M., Gibbs, G.V. (2005). Electron density distribution and bond critical point properties for forsterite, Mg2SiO4, determined with synchrotron single crystal X-ray diffraction data. Physics and Chemistry of Minerals 32, 301–313.
